title: How 8 cups of tea prove you're not guessing
description:
Muriel Bristol, a scientist at Rothamsted in England, said she could taste whether the milk or the tea went into the cup first. Ronald Fisher's test: eight cups, four of each, in random order, and she knows it's four and four. There are 70 ways to pick four cups out of eight, so a pure guesser picks the right four only 1 time in 70 (1.4%). Three out of four sounds convincing, but a guesser gets three or more one time in four (17 of 70), so only a perfect score counts. She reportedly got all eight right, and Fisher used the test in his 1935 book The Design of Experiments.

Numbers checked in code: the counts exactly and 100,000 simulated guessers. Sources: Wikipedia, Lady tasting tea; Muriel Bristol.

social_caption: Eight cups of tea, and a guesser has a 1 in 70 chance. How Ronald Fisher tested a claim that seemed impossible to test.
facts_checked: One cup: a guesser is right 1 in 2; C(8,4) = 70 ways to pick 4 of 8; exactly 3 of 4 right: 16 ways, 3 or more: 17 (24%, about one time in 4); all right: 1 in 70 = 1.4%, under Fisher's 5%; 100,000 simulated guessers: 1.36% all right, 24.1% three or more (verify.py)

Muriel Bristol claimed she could tell whether tea or milk was added first; eight cups, four of each, random order, method disclosed; 1 in 70; only all correct rejects at 5%; Fisher's The Design of Experiments (1935); per Salsburg (H. Fairfield Smith), she identified all eight (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_tasting_tea)

Bristol worked at Rothamsted Experimental Station from 1919; the test happened 'one day at Rothamsted'; Fisher doubted it; she correctly identified all eight cups (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muriel_Bristol)

beats.say: Eight cups of tea can prove you're not just guessing.
One cup proves nothing. A pure guesser gets it right half the time.
England, at a farm research lab. Muriel Bristol says she can taste whether the milk went in first. Ronald Fisher doesn't buy it.
So pour eight cups. Four milk first, four tea first. Shuffle them, and tell her it's four and four.
She picks the four milk-first cups. There are 70 ways to pick four of eight. Only one is all right.
But what if she gets three out of four? Sounds convincing.
A guesser does that one time in four. So set the rule before she tastes: all four, or it proves nothing.
She got all eight. By luck, that's one in 70. Fisher put the test in his 1935 book on experiments.
